posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I was reading the new question/answer session on G307 by Michael and John, and I think it was John who made the interesting comment that CrVI is orangish, while CrIII is bluish.

On some of my recent tests, I noticed that some of my processed DCG layers, the really bright images, are definitely bluish, while the dimmer ones came out clear. That is, if I place the finished holograms on a white surface, and light it so that I don't see any diffraction from the image (just the light bouncing back through the emulsion, at a glancing angle) it is definitely bluish or purplish. Has anyone else noticed this?

It turned out that ageing the plates for only one day was not enough in my case. I stored some coated plates in the refrigerator for two weeks, and made two exposures (using these) last weekend. Much brighter holograms were produced, for some reason, compared to the same batch of plates that aged for only one day. Don't know why.

The variables weren't changed that much, as far as I can tell. I kept the humidity in the 50 to 60% range everywhere. The literature states quite clearly that DCG is most sensitive in a hot, moist environment, so if the two-week old plates had "dried" more than the day-old plates, then I would have a tough time connecting dryness to more effective crosslinking, so I doubt if that's the reason. The brighter holograms did seem to come out a bit more broadband, but I don't think that explains the large increase in brightness. There is an old paper by Schlesinger/Unterseher which says they got optimal results when the DCG mixture was 3 weeks old, which was exactly the time lapse after mixing in my case. ("Dichromated Gelatin Holograms: A Reliable Method.")

Michael, I was just using standard DCG (not G307).

Patrick, I was using transmitted white light to see the blue color. Colored substances usually show a similar color effect in transmission as they do in reflection, under white light. So blue will usually look blue whether in transmission or reflection, under white light illumination. (Here I am only talking about substances, not anything to due with diffraction). There are notable exceptions, however, and the so-called "top tone" and "undertone" can look very different.

Dave, I still don't think this is due to Bragg planes or diffraction. It's just like a faint stain on the emulsion. It is not at all angular-selective. Just like a faint blue or purple dye. posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hey Joe, not sure if your following the alcohol thread but I have come to the conclusion that the there are hardly any voids in the crosslinked areas and the amount of voids and their size there is completely dependeng on the amount of crosslinking in that area. I would assum many to be quite close to the size of a molecule or two of water. But in the unexposed and much less crosslinked but crosslinked to some extent because of dark reaction, fixing/hardening, post baking and the such, there is much more room for larger collections of water molecules and it is in this unexposed region that the voids and cracks are formed that everyone talks about and has electron photographed.

For some reason this just makes more sense to me. 

PS: I thought I was wong once, but I was mistaken....LOL.

But lets look at this logically;

* There has to be something in the unexposed regions (layers in a reflection) to keep the exposed regions from collapsing down on one another.

* It would not make sense that the higher index of refraction exposed layer has air voids in it. That would lower it's index of refraction. 

* It does make sense the the expose area has a higher concentration of gelatin and thus is higher index of refraction but the unexposed area has the voids and cracks of air which lower is index of refraction.

The real key in a very bright hologram, as I have been pushing, it so get as least dense as possible with the most air in the unexposed regions to give a greater delta index of refraction between it and the dense exposed gelatin layer.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
John, I made a typo when I said some voids also form in the unexposed areas. What I meant to say is that some voids also form in the exposed (hardened) areas (at least, so I think). But I pretty much agree with everything you said.

According to what I've read, though, some voids do form in the hardened areas as well, but they are much fewer in number. (This is according to the Russian work on SHSG, which I assume is quite similar to DCG in this respect.) Of course, we don't want any voids to be there because this will reduce index modulation. But I have yet to see any good electron micrographs of hardened areas DCG to see if they are free of any voids or not. It's just my assumption that the process is not perfect, and some voids will appear there anyway (I could be wrong).

The way I see it, soft gelatin simply has a propensity for voids when processed in the DCG manner. It would of course be best if we could eliminate the voids that may form in the so-called hardened areas. It's just my assumption that the hardened areas are not perfectly hardened, and some voids probably appear there as well.
